As a direction particle, へ is read “e”, just as the particle は is read “wa”. どこ へ = “doko e”.
All the days end in “-yōbi”, with a long o: ge-tsu-YOH-bi. Don’t shorten it!
しゅう = “shuu”, a single long sound, not “shi-yu-u”. ひこうき = hi-koh-ki.
1. Three verbs of movement
When you use it
you leave where you are for another place
someone comes towards where YOU are
you go back “home” (your house, your country, your office)
My mum is coming from Japan (here, to me).
English speakers say “I’m going home” and reach for いきます. In Japanese, when it’s YOUR home, use かえります: うち へ かえります.
2. Direction: へ or に
The place you’re going to is marked with へ (read “e”) or に. At your level, they mean exactly the same.
I’m going to Kyoto.
I’m going to Kyoto (the same).
へ stresses the DIRECTION (“towards”), に the DESTINATION (“to”). Both are correct with いきます / きます / かえります.
“Nowhere”: どこ へ も + negative. E.g.: どこ へ も いきません = I’m not going anywhere.
3. How? The particle で (means)
You’ve seen で as “the place where you do something”. It has a second role: the MEANS, the instrument. For transport: VEHICLE で.
by train
by bus
by plane
by car
on foot ⚠️ no で
How are you getting there?
“あるいて” already means “walking”, so you don’t put で after it.
4. With whom? The particle と
と after a person = “together with”. You’ve also learned と as “and” between nouns (パン と たまご). Context tells you which it is.
I’m going to the shop with a friend.
I’m going alone.
A polite invitation: ～ません か (won’t you…?). いっしょ に いきません か = Won’t you come with me? It’s gentler than ～ましょう (let’s…).
5. The days of the week and “when?”

With days of the week you CAN use に: どようび に いきます. With きょう / あした / らいしゅう / せんしゅう you DON’T (the rule from chapter 4).
The normal sentence order: WHO は — WHEN — WITH WHOM と — HOW で — WHERE へ — VERB.
On Saturday I’m going to Kyoto by train with a friend.
Your mother is coming to see you. Which verb?

バレンシア へ の たび — The trip to Valencia
Saturday morning, seven o’clock. Mihai is at the station.
Ana hasn’t come yet. The train is at half past seven.
At twenty past seven, Ana came running.
“Sorry! The metro was slow!”
They both got on the train. The train is very fast.
From Madrid to Valencia it’s about two hours.
On the train, Mihai read a Japanese book.
Ana looked out of the window. “Wow, there are so many orange trees!”
At half past nine they arrived in Valencia. The sky is blue and it’s warm.
From the station to the sea they went by bus. It took twenty minutes.
There were lots of people at the seaside. There were children and dogs too.
At lunchtime, the two of them ate paella.
Valencian paella is famous. It was delicious.
“Mihai, are you resting at home? Or are you swimming in the sea?”
“The sea, of course!”
In the afternoon, the two of them swam in the sea. Then they walked around the city.
There was an old church and a big market.
At the market, Ana bought a present for Yuki’s mother.
It’s a little box of oranges. “Are there oranges in Japan?” “There are. But they’re expensive.”
On Sunday evening, the two of them went back to Madrid.
On the train, Mihai fell asleep straight away.
Ana looked at Mihai and laughed. “Resting at home, eh?”
On Monday morning an email came from Yuki.
“How was Valencia? Show me the photos, please!”
